text: A contract is only discharged when the parties have performed their exact and entire obligations. Assess the validity of this statement.
title: A contract is only discharged when the parties have performed their exact and entire obligations. Assess the validity of this statement.
msText: A contract is only discharged when the parties have performed their exact and entire obligations. Assess the validity of this statement. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding • The entire/strict performance rule; entire obligation must be performed completely and in its entirety, Cutter v Powell, Re Moore and Co. Ltd and Landauer and Co • Exceptions to the strict rule: – Severable/divisible contract – where a contract can be seen in separate parts, non-completion of one part is not a breach of the whole, Ritchie v Atkinson, Taylor v Webb – Substantial performance – where a party completes substantially if not precisely all parts of the contract. Payment will be required less the cost to rectify the imperfections, Hoenig v Isaacs, Bolton v Mahadeva, Young v Thames Properties Ltd – Voluntary acceptance of part-performance – where one party has agreed that the other party need not complete the entire contract, Sumpter v Hedges – Prevention of performance, Planche v Colburn – Timing – performance must occur at the time agreed in the contract (time is of the essence), Union Eagle Ltd v Golden Achievement Ltd – Tender of performance -iIf a party offers to perform their contractual obligations but the other party refuses, the offering party may be discharged, Startup v Macdonald – Vicarious performance – performance by a third party may discharge a contract if the contract doesn’t require personal performance, British Waggon Co v Lea & Co Credit any other relevant content AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: • Entire performance is still the starting point in any dispute and, in a dispute, the court will expect exact and complete performance • If there is a substantial lack of performance the courts will not consider the contract complete and the strict rule will apply • Substantial performance allows a party to avoid the strict rule as a party can escape, for example, without completing all the required work. However, there is a problem defining ‘substantial’. The strict rule is avoided • Whilst substantial may allow for the strict rule to be avoided the court will use their discretion to reach a just and fair decision through quantum meruit • Voluntary acceptance of part-performance appears to allow parties to avoid the strict rule but, the requirement of voluntary acceptance means that if there is no agreement the strict rule will apply • In part-performance the voluntary acceptance (consent) must acknowledge that the defaulting party is entitled to be paid for what they have completed so far, as the agreement was made without undue influence. In the absence of such the entire rule will prevail • The innocent party is protected in part-performance. If the innocent party has no option but to accept the work partially done, this is not considered consent to part-performance and the strict rule will be applied • Categorising a contract as severable allows a party to avoid the entire performance. However, the defendant is required to show that each part of the contract can be discharged separately. Credit any other relevant analysis and application and evaluation AO1 AO2 AO3

text: Discuss the extent to which the rebuttable presumptions in intention to create legal relations lead to uncertainty.
title: Discuss the extent to which the rebuttable presumptions in intention to create legal relations lead to uncertainty.
msText: Discuss the extent to which the rebuttable presumptions in intention to create legal relations lead to uncertainty. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding Social and domestic arrangements – rebuttable presumption that there is no intention to create legal relations, Balfour v Balfour, Jones v Padavatton • Presumption may be rebutted: – Where there is a reliance on the promise, Parker v Clarke – Where contrary evidence to rebut can be produced, Merritt v Merritt – Where financial security is at risk, Simpkins v Pays • Commercial and business agreements – very strong rebuttable presumption that there is intention to create legal relations • Presumptions may be rebutted: – If clear words are used to show no legal intent, Jones v Vernon Pools, Confetti Records v Warner Music UK Ltd – Where an honour pledge clause is inserted, Rose and Frank Co v JR Crompton and Bros Ltd – Where the words used are not clear enough to amount to a specific promise, Kleinwort Benson v Malaysia Mining – A statement indicating no previous legal liability may be seen as merely explaining the offer which is now being made, Edwards v Skyways. Credit any other relevant content AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: • Uncertainty is caused when there are conflicting decisions. For example, in Parker v Clarke the parties relied on the agreement made with the older couple and the court found that as they had given up their security there was an intention. The daughter in Jones v Padavatton did a similar thing but the presumption was not rebutted – this case divided the Court of Appeal • There is uncertainty in gambling contracts for example the bingo, lottery cases. Whilst the cases are similar the decision vary • There is uncertainty as to what ‘contrary evidence’ might be needed to rebut the social and domestic arrangements presumption. There are no clear guidelines making giving advice difficult • The starting points for business agreements is that there is legal intent – this creates certainty • There may be uncertainty in terms of a ‘gentleman's agreement’ as seen in Blue v Ashley • Uncertainty may arise when a court is deciding clarity in wording. It will be for the court to decide rather than the parties. By deciding each case on its own facts may be considered to cause uncertainty to parties • There is uncertainty when cases fall into an ‘in between’ a social and commercial agreement. In such cases the presumption will vary on which side the decision is made – who has the best argument – Sadler v Reynolds. Credit any other relevant analysis and application and evaluation AO1 AO2 AO3

text: Benji is trying to sell his car and hears that Clarice might be interested in buying one. He writes and posts a letter to Clarice offering to sell the car to her for £10 000. Benji’s letter tells Clarice that he needs a reply by 30 May. On 28 May, Clarice hears from a mutual friend that Benji has agreed to sell his car to a car dealer. Nevertheless, Clarice posts a letter of acceptance the same day, agreeing to buy the car for £10 000. Benji receives the letter from Clarice on 29 May. Assess Benji’s potential contractual liability to Clarice and to the car dealer.

Indicative content Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding • Identify the issues of offer, invitation to treat, revocation and acceptance. • Show an understanding of the postal rule (Adams v Lindsell) and the conditions of its use (Holwell Securities v Hughes). • Demonstrate knowledge of revocation of an offer (Byrne v Van Tienhovan) including by a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds). Credit any other relevant case cited for AO1. AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation • Show whether there was a firm offer by Benji to sell the car and comment on any significance of Clarice’s reply being received prior to the 30 May. • Consider the significance of Clarice’s awareness that the offer had been withdrawn. • Be given credit for any possible suggestion of remedies available to Clarice or the car dealer depending on line of reasoning. Accept all valid responses. AO1 AO2 AO3

text: On 1 July, Spool Fashions (SF) enters into a contract with Tara to make her a dress for her wedding. They agree a collection date of 1 August. Tara makes an initial payment of £500 and agrees to pay the balance of £1500 when the dress is collected. One week later, Tara regrets her decision to spend such a large amount of money. She telephones SF to cancel the order and to ask for her deposit back. SF is busy completing other contracts and has not yet begun to make Tara’s dress. However, Tara is told that she can no longer change her mind and that the dress will be ready to collect as agreed. The next day, a gas explosion causes damage to SF’s workshop and destroys its equipment. SF’s workshop is officially declared as unsafe and its use is prohibited for two months until repairs have been carried out. SF is forced to suspend business. Advise SF and Tara of their respective contractual rights and obligations throughout the course of these events.

Tara makes an initial payment of £500 and agrees to pay the balance of £1500 when the dress is collected. One week later, Tara regrets her decision to spend such a large amount of money. She telephones SF to cancel the order and to ask for her deposit back. SF is busy completing other contracts and has not yet begun to make Tara’s dress. However, Tara is told that she can no longer change her mind and that the dress will be ready to collect as agreed. The next day, a gas explosion causes damage to SF’s workshop and destroys its equipment. SF’s workshop is officially declared as unsafe and its use is prohibited for two months until repairs have been carried out. SF is forced to suspend business. Advise SF and Tara of their respective contractual rights and obligations throughout the course of these events.
msText: Advise SF and Tara of their respective contractual rights and obligations throughout the course of these events. Use Table A to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding • Identify the issues of anticipatory breach and frustration of contract. • Explain the difference between anticipatory breach and actual breach (Hochster v De la Tour) and outline the choices available to the innocent party (Avery v Bowden). • Define the doctrine of frustration, explain how it may occur (Taylor v Caldwell) and outline the effects of it with reference to the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943. Credit any other relevant case cited for AO1. AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation • Recognise Tara’s breach as anticipatory giving SF the right to sue immediately or wait until 1 August. • Recognise SF’s decision to affirm the contract because the dress can be completed without Tara’s co-operation and consider whether SF has a genuine interest in doing this by evaluating if Lord Reid’s restrictions stated in White and Carter (Councils) Ltd would apply. • Demonstrate how the gas explosion frustrates the contract, and show how the LR(FC)A 1943 would likely apportion loss. Accept all valid responses. AO1 AO2 AO3

text: Assess the extent to which the use of innominate terms has resulted in a significant level of uncertainty in contract law.
title: Assess the extent to which the use of innominate terms has resulted in a significant level of uncertainty in contract law.
msText: Assess the extent to which the use of innominate terms has resulted in a significant level of uncertainty in contract law. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding • Show understanding of the difference between a condition and warranty (Poussard v Spiers and Pond, Bettini v Gye). • Explain how this traditional approach was challenged by the creation of the innominate term (The Hong Kong Fir Case). AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation Responses should acknowledge the law’s dislike of uncertainty and select arguments to show how this flaw may manifest itself with the use of the innominate term. These may include: • The innocent party’s difficulty in knowing how to react until the effects of the breach have played out. • The danger of pursuing expensive and ultimately futile litigation (The Chikuma). • By disturbing established commercial assumptions. For example in shipping contracts ‘readiness to load’ clauses are always treated by the courts to be conditions (The Mihalis Angelos). Responses should argue that there are in fact benefits to its use which outweigh the potential for uncertainty. These may include: • Creating flexibility in the law by giving the court a wider view of the contract with the chance to create the right decision (Hong Kong Fir). • Preventing breach for a trivial reason (The Hansa Nord) or to escape unwanted contracts (Reardon Smith Line v Hansen-Tangen). • Disputing whether it is any less certain than the traditional approach (Schuler AG v Wickman Machine Tools Sales Ltd). Accept all valid responses. AO1 AO2 AO3

text: English law aims to strike a balance between the freedom to contract and the need to protect people who are unable to protect themselves. Assess the extent to which minors are protected when entering into contracts.
title: English law aims to strike a balance between the freedom to contract and the need to protect people who are unable to protect themselves. Assess the extent to which minors are protected when entering into contracts.
msText: English law aims to strike a balance between the freedom to contract and the need to protect people who are unable to protect themselves. Assess the extent to which minors are protected when entering into contracts. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding Responses should show knowledge and understanding of the types of contract that may bind minors by: • Outlining contracts for necessaries (Nash v Inman) and beneficial contracts (De Francesco v Barnum). • Describing the nature of voidable contracts (Corpe v Overton). • Referring to key sections of the Minors’ Contract Act 1987. AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation Responses may offer the following arguments to support the premise that the law gives minors the freedom to make contracts: • Necessary contracts mean minors are not disadvantaged and can acquire basic requirements of life. • Beneficial contracts allow minors the chance to make their way in life by receiving an education, training or employment. • Voidable contracts provide a workable arrangement between minors and adults dealing fairly with them. These arguments should be balanced by an appreciation of the law’s paternalistic approach towards minors’ contracts. For example: • Minors are only bound to pay for necessary goods and services and even then only at a reasonable price. • Minors can escape contracts of employment if terms are on the whole onerous or can be released from voidable contracts in certain circumstances. • The limited remedies given to an adult in comparison. Accept all valid responses. AO1 AO2 AO3

text: An award of damages may be limited by causation, remoteness and mitigation. Justify the view that these limitations are based on a desire to be fair to both parties.
title: An award of damages may be limited by causation, remoteness and mitigation. Justify the view that these limitations are based on a desire to be fair to both parties.
msText: An award of damages may be limited by causation, remoteness and mitigation. Justify the view that these limitations are based on a desire to be fair to both parties. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding Responses should: • Outline the issues of causation (Quinn v Burch Brothers (Builders) Ltd). • Outline the issue of remoteness of damage (Hadley v Baxendale). • Outline the duty to mitigate loss (Brace v Calder). Responses can be given credit for any brief outline of the aims of damages as a remedy but no credit should be given to responses which discuss measures of quantifying or calculating loss. AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation Responses should address the assertion in the question and may discuss the following: • Fairness dictates that there should be some link between the breach of contract and any consequential loss. • Given the compensatory aim of damages it is only fair that an innocent party should not benefit from any breach. • It is not just or even practical to make the defendant liable for every consequential loss which arises from the breach. • Whether mitigation reduces the scope of the protection given to the innocent party. Accept all valid responses. AO1 AO2 AO3

text: Henry wants to sell his car. Ian knows this and so writes to Henry on the 23 May offering to buy it. The letter reads: ‘I will give you £4000 for the car and no more. If I hear nothing to the contrary from you by 1 June, I will assume the car is mine at that price.’ When he receives Ian’s letter, Henry doesn’t reply as he wants more than £4000 for the car. On 26 May, Henry posts separate but identical letters to Jane and Kim, offering to sell his car for £5000. On 28 May, they both receive Henry’s letter which clearly states, ‘any acceptance must reach me at my home address before 1 June’. On 29 May, Jane writes a letter agreeing to Henry’s asking price and goes to her local post office. She pays the postage fee, obtains proof of posting and posts the letter. Although the letter is correctly addressed it never arrives at Henry’s home. On the evening of 31 May, Kim goes to Henry’s house and tells him that she will pay the £5000 asking price for the car. Henry tells Kim he will deliver the car to her the following morning and collect payment from her. Advise Henry of his contractual liability, if any, towards Ian, Jane and Kim in these circumstances.

msText: Advise Leo whether he can terminate each contract and claim damages. Use Table A to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding • Conditions: Very important terms – they go to the root of the agreement. Contract cannot be performed if the term is breached, Poussards v Spiers and Pond Remedy – repudiate and claim damages. • Warranties: Minor terms When breached the contract can continue, Bettini v Gye Remedy – claim damages • Innominate Term Covers situations where a term cannot be categorised as a condition or a warranty. Court will consider the consequence of the breach, Hong Kong Fir Case Innocent party will only be able to treat the contact at an end if the whole benefit has been deprived, Reardon Smith Line v Yngvar Hansen-Tangen Court will consider an expressly stated term but if the breach is minor there will be no right to repudiate the contract, Schuler v Wickman. Credit any other relevant information AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: Taylor training the new staff: ● Taylor has breached an express term • Training for five days would be crucial to the running of the new cafe when it opened • Training of staff would be a condition as it would be considered a major term going to the heart of the agreement • The term would be such an important term that the contact between Leo and Taylor would be rendered meaningless if not fulfilled • Leo will be at liberty to end the contract with Taylor and claim damages Anika and the supply of coffee: • Anika has breached an expressed term • Anika is contracted to supply 15  10 kg bags of coffee but instead delivers 30  5 kg bags • Supplying the coffee in different size bags does not deprive Leo of the whole benefit of the contract – the main purpose of the agreement was to be supplied with 150 kg of coffee • The contract can continue, this would be a breach of warranty • Leo would be unable to end the contract with Anika but can seek damages. Riley arriving late to clean: • Riley has breached an express term • Address whether arriving late deprives Leo of the whole benefit of the contract • The court may consider this as an innominate term • In such a situation the court will consider the consequence of Riley’s breach • The breach does not appear to be so bad that it is fair on both parties to end the contract ● Conclude that the breach (i) is sufficiently serious, and the Leo can end the contact and seek damages or (ii) is not serious enough that Leo can end the contract, he can only seek damages Credit any other relevant information AO1 AO2 AO3

text: The point at which an offer ends is uncertain. Assess the validity of this view.
title: The point at which an offer ends is uncertain. Assess the validity of this view.
msText: The point at which an offer ends is uncertain. Assess the validity of this view. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding The ways an offer can end include: ● Acceptance/rejection ends an offer. ● Revocation: this must be communicated, Byrne v Van Tienhoven can be communicated by a reliable third party, Dickenson v Dodds. must take place at any time before acceptance, Routledge v Grant Offeror is not at liberty to revoke a unilateral agreement when acceptance is on-going, Errington v Errington Woods • By lapsing after a reasonable amount of time, Ramsgate Victoria Hotel v Montifoire ● A counteroffer. This destroys the original offer, Hyde v Wrench • A request for information does not destroy the original offer, Stevenson Jacques & Co v Mclean • Death of the offeree brings the offer to an end. • Death of the offeror; acceptance can still take place until the offeree is notified of the death. If the contract is for personal service, the offer will end, Bradbury v Morgan. ● Failure of a pre-condition, Financing v Stimson Credit any other relevant information AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: Responses may offer the following arguments to support the premise that the ways in which an offer can end are vague and lack certainty: • The rule that revocation must be communicated is clear and certain • The rule that revocation must be communicated may cause uncertainty as the rule is so different to acceptance • Revocation can take place at any time before acceptance, but the offeree ‘should’ be informed of the revocation. It is not always clear of the need to inform the offeree or whether the offer does stay open without consideration being provided • The rules regarding revoking a unilateral offer are clear, the offeror is not permitted to end the contract if the expected conduct is being executed • Who is considered a ‘reliable’ third party lacks clarity • What amounts to a ‘reasonable’ lapse of time is vague and seems to depend on too many vague factors? • The difference between a counteroffer and a request for further information may cause confusion and can lack clarity/certainty • It is not definite that the death of the offeror will terminate an offer. There are circumstances when it will not, this may lead to uncertainty. Credit any other relevant information AO1 AO2 AO3

text: Assess the extent to which the limited use of the remedy of specific performance prevents justice from being achieved.
title: Assess the extent to which the limited use of the remedy of specific performance prevents justice from being achieved.
msText: Assess the extent to which the limited use of the remedy of specific performance prevents justice from being achieved. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding Specific performance: ● Equitable remedy awarded at the discretion of the court. • Specific performance is where a court issues an order requiring a party to perform an act. ● will not be granted for a number of reasons including: If damages would be adequate If the order would inevitably force a company into liquidation – Airport Industrial GP Ltd v Heathrow Airport Ltd If constant supervision of the court is required, Ryan v Mutual Tontine In contracts of personal service – Page One Records Ltd v Britton. To enforce an unfair contract, Walters v Morgan If it will cause the defendant hardship, Patel v Ali. In the absence of mutuality, Price v Strange, Flight v Bolland Where the D behaved inequitably Credit any other relevant information AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: Responses may offer the following arguments to support: • Whilst there is a restrictive approach it does not prohibit the grant of specific performance • As an equitable remedy it allows equity to step in adding both fairness and justice. It will be granted when it is fair and just to do so • The restrictive approach still allows for flexibility and discretion • Justice is served when such a restrictive approach is taken as it allows for the damages to remain the primary remedy. This is the most appropriate in the vast majority of conflicts • Justice is achieved as the remedy cannot be used if it will harm the defendant – Airport Industrial GP Ltd v Heathrow Airport Ltd • Is too restrictive as it is only really used when the nature of the dispute is unique. However, that allows for justice – money cannot replace everything • Justice is not achieved as the burden is on the claimant to demonstrate why damages would be an insufficient remedy. This is a heavy burden • Justice is not achieved – it is so rarely used • Justice is not achieved due to the narrowness of the remedy – it is only available in exceptional circumstances; where goods are of a unique nature and cannot be replaced in an ‘available market’ meaning an award of damages is inadequate – Behnke v Bede Shipping Co Ltd, Falcke v Gray, Sale of land – Adderley v Dixon or an obligation to pay money to a third party – Beswick v Beswick • Justice is achieved as it will only be granted if the court is sure that they are capable of supervising performance and ensure that the order can be carried out. It would be unjust to make an order that could not be enforced • The restriction on availability in employment contracts may be considered unjust when a specialist employee cannot be ordered to perform as per the contract. However, it could be seen as infringing personal freedom to make someone work for an employer they don’t wish to • There still exists flexibility in employment and can be used to compel employer to reinstate an employee Credit any other relevant information AO1 AO2 AO3

text: The common law distinction between representations and terms is vital but frequently unclear. Evaluate the factors considered when deciding whether a pre-contractual statement is a representation or a term.
title: The common law distinction between representations and terms is vital but frequently unclear. Evaluate the factors considered when deciding whether a pre-contractual statement is a representation or a term.
msText: The common law distinction between representations and terms is vital but frequently unclear. Evaluate the factors considered when deciding whether a pre- contractual statement is a representation or a term. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding Whether or not a statement is incorporated as a term has been developed by judges and depends upon a number of different factors including: • The time between making the statement and formation of the contract – the longer the time difference between the two, the less likely the statement will be incorporated, Routledge v McKay. • The importance attached to the representation – the more importance attached to the statement the more likely it is that it is a term, Bannerman v White. • Special knowledge or skill – statements made by parties with specific expertise can be relied upon, Oscar Chess v Williams, Dick Bentley Productions v Harold Smith (Motors) • Reduction of terms in writing – Routledge v Grant, Birch v Paramount Estates (Liverpool) Ltd ● Incorporation by signature, L’Estrange v Graucob • Terms implied by trade or professional custom – ‘custom hardens into right’, Schawel v Reade ● Parol evidence rule, Webster v Cecil Credit any other relevant information AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: Responses should address the assertion in the question and may discuss the following: • Rules on incorporation have been developed by judges through the common law in an attempt to produce a consistent approach and as a result provide justice • However, whether or not a statement is incorporated as a term depends upon many different factors – this produces uncertainty and does not guarantee justice • Incorporating statements as a term does not provide justice as it allows for departure from the principle of freedom to contract in certain circumstances • Clear as justice is provided where the term has great importance, i.e., in situations where the innocent party would not have entered the contract but for the statement. If this was not the case, the intention of the party would be ignored • Certainty is provided for the ‘innocent/weaker’ party when oral information is given by a person with expertise. It is fair that a party can rely on these statements. If this were not the case, salespeople would be at liberty to make outrageous statements • Certainty is provided by the fact that a party is bound if they sign a document/tick the terms and conditions box online. This stops parties avoiding a ‘bad’ contract. The party is given the opportunity to read the terms before signing • Certainty is provided to, for example, a seller. If they make a statement and there is a significant gap between the making of that statement and the contract, it is fair to say the statement is not incorporated into the contract. However, there is no rule as to the time delay, it will be based on the objective test which produces uncertainty • The parol evidence rule provides an element of certainty as only written terms will be incorporated even where there are additional oral statements made. It will be assumed that anything omitted was not intended to be included. To do otherwise would create uncertainty • The parol evidence does not provide certainty as there are too many exceptions which produces uncertainty • Certainty is provided as courts are moving away from a ‘literal’ approach to one of the ‘purposive’ approach. The courts will look at, among other things, the commercial purpose of the transaction including pre- contractual negotiations. Credit any other relevant information AO1 AO2 AO3

At the end of the film, Jada goes to collect her coat, but it is missing. As she is leaving the cinema, she slips on a spilt drink which has not been cleaned up by a member of staff. Jada breaks her arm as she falls. Two months later, Jada asks to cancel her membership because she has obtained a job abroad. Jada makes a claim against ABL. The company states that it is not liable for her losses and she cannot cancel her membership. Advise Jada and ABL of their respective contractual rights and obligations
msText: Advise Jada and ABL of their respective contractual rights and obligations. Use Table A to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding Common law control of exclusion clauses: • Is the agreement in writing, L’Estrange v Graucob, Curtis v Chemical Cleaning and Dyeing Co Ltd • Reasonably notice, Olley v Marlborough Court Hotel, Chapelton v Barry UDC, • Previous course of dealing, McCutcheon v David MacBrayne Ltd Statutory control of exclusion clauses Consumer Right Act 2015: • S.61 - covers consumer contracts • S.62 - consumer contract terms and notices must be fair.  The term will be considered unfair if there is a significant imbalance in the parties’ rights and obligations under the contract to the detriment of the consumer • Schedule 2 lists terms which may be regarded as unfair • S.65 - trader cannot exclude or restrict liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence • S68 - requires the trader to ensure that a written term is transparent i.e. written in plain intelligible language and legible Credit any other relevant content AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: Ticking the terms and conditions box: • Jada had actual knowledge of the terms and conditions at the time of entering into the contract - they were set out clearly • It does not matter that Jada did not read the terms • Jada is bound by the terms and conditions. • Missing coat: • To avoid liability ABL will need to show that the notice is clear and brought to the customers attention • The exclusion notice is clear - it is a large notice • By leaving the coat, Jada appears to have accepted the risk • ABL will be able to rely on the sign • Broken arm: • ABL is not permitted to avoid liability for personal injury arising from their negligence • Not cleaning up a spilt drink would be considered a negligent act • Conclude that ABL will not be able to exclude liability for Jada’s broken arm Cancelling the gym membership: • The terms must be considered fair (s62) and not contrary to the requirement of good faith • The term is transparent and written in intelligible language and legible • Credit any sensible conclusion as to whether ABL are able to rely on the clause relating to membership cancellation. Credit any other relevant analysis and application and evaluation AO1 AO2 AO3 Answer

title: Adam lives in a house bought by his parents. He and his parents have a written agreement that states that Adam can stay there until he has enough money to buy his own house. It also states that he must keep the house clean and tidy. When his parents visit, the house is very untidy, so they tell him to move out immediately. Adam is now living with a friend. He sees that the local pizza company is running a promotion, giving a free dessert with every pizza ordered. Adam orders and pays for a pizza, but when it arrives there is no dessert. The delivery driver tells Adam that the company has run out of free desserts. Advise whether intention to create legal relations is present in these agreements.
msText: Advise whether intention to create legal relations is present in these agreements. Use Table A to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: AO1 Knowledge and understanding Social and domestic arrangements • There is a rebuttable presumption that agreements made between family members have no intention to create legal relations, Jones v Padavatton, Balfour v Balfour • The presumptions can be rebutted: – Where the parties are no longer acting on the basis of love and affection, Merritt v Merritt – Where the parties have acted in reliance on the promise, Parker v Clark – Where financial security is at risk, Simpkins v Pays, Wilson v Burnett – Seriousness of the situation, Darke v Strout Commercial and business agreements • There is a very strong rebuttable presumption that there is intention to create legal relations in commercial agreements, Esso v commissioners for Esso Petroleum Co Ltd v CCE, Carlill v The Carbolic Smoke Ball Co Ltd, McGowan v Radio Buxton • The presumptions can be rebutted: – If clear words are used to show no legal intent, Jones v Vernon Pools, Confetti Records v Warner Music UK Ltd – Where an honour pledge clause inserted, Rose and Frank Co v JR Crompton and Bros Ltd – Where the words used are not clear enough to amount to a specific promise, Kleinwort Benson v Malaysia Mining – A statement indicating no previous legal liability may be seen as merely explaining the offer which is now being made, Edwards v Skyways Credit any other relevant content AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: Adam being told to leave the house immediately: • This is a family arrangement as per Jones v Padavatton • The presumption is that there will be non-intention to create legal relations • However, the presumption can be rebutted with evidence to the contrary • The written document setting out the intentions may be enough to rebut the presumption of no intention • If Adam has acted in reliance this may also be enough to rebut the presumption • Conclude that the presumption of no intention to create legal relations will be rebutted OR • will not be rebutted Adam and the free dessert: • This is a commercial agreement • There is a very strong presumption that commercial contracts are legally binding • This appears to be a pizza company offering a free dessert and this would be done in order to promote a business • This would be enough to conclude that the commercial presumption applies • Conclude that the commercial presumption has not been rebutted Credit any other relevant analysis and application and evaluation AO1 AO2 AO3

text: Discuss the extent to which the rules for communicating acceptance need to be modernised.
title: Discuss the extent to which the rules for communicating acceptance need to be modernised.
msText: Discuss the extent to which the rules for communicating acceptance need to be modernised. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding • Acceptance is the positive and unqualified confirmation of all the terms of the offer • Acceptance must correspond exactly with the offer - mirror image rule • Acceptance must be effectively communicated and can be in any form; writing, oral, conduct, Yates v Pulleyn • Acceptance is effective as soon as it is received, Entores v Miles Far East Corp • The acceptance must be communicated to the offeror - silence does not constitute acceptance, Felthouse v Bindley, Inland Revenue Commissioners v Fry • Acceptance may be waived - unilateral offers, Carlill v The Carbolic Smoke Ball Co Ltd • Methods of communication: – Non-instantaneous - postal rule, acceptance on positing - Adams v Lindsell – Instantaneous (phone/email/text etc) - treated as a face to face and general communication rule and applies as per Entores reaffirmed in Brinkibon Stahag. – Communicating during business hours, The Brimnes, Thomas v BPE Solicitors – Battle of the Forms - last shot - Butler Machine Tool Ltd v Ex-Cell-O Corp, TRW v Panasonic Credit any other relevant content AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: • The rule on silence is confusing and therefore may need modernising. In Felthouse the nephew had asked the auctioneer holding the horse to remove it from the auction - he was not silent.  However, if silence amounted to acceptance, people may become entrapped into contracts • Another problem with the silence rule is that it is not absolute as per Vitol SA v Norelf Ltd and The Hannah Blumenthal • Acceptance rules have been modernised. The Unsolicited Goods and Services Act ensures that contracts are not imposed on unsuspecting people.  The Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013 states that unsolicited goods sent to consumers can be treated as an unconditional gift immediately. • The postal rule needs modernising or to be removed.  It made sense when it was first used as there were limited alternatives available for long distance communication. • The rule has limited use as it only applies to the Royal Mail, a privatised company. It seems unjust that it does not apply to other private mail companies. • The postal rule needs modernising as it can appear unfair and can cause uncertainty. If the offeror does not receive the letter of acceptance, because, for example, the postal service has lost it - how do they know there is acceptance?  The fairness and appropriateness of this rule in the 21st Century is questionable particularly as so few people use the postal service. • Modernisation may be required due to Brexit. Clarity is required as to the relevance of, for example, the Electronic Commerce (EC Directive) Regulations • Modernisation needs to happen as the communication rules are failing to address more modern methods of communication as seen in Thomas and Gander v BPE Solicitors. Deciding each case on its particular facts makes it difficult for lawyers to give advice • Modernisation is proposed in the Law Commission Electronic execution of documents report. Credit any other relevant analysis and application and evaluation AO1 AO2 AO3 Answer

text: The award of specific performance and injunction guarantee justice is served. Assess the validity of this statement.
title: The award of specific performance and injunction guarantee justice is served. Assess the validity of this statement.
msText: The award of specific performance and injunction guarantee justice is served. Assess the validity of this statement. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding Specific performance: • Where a court issues an order requiring a party to perform an act • May be granted when the subject matter of the contract is unique, and damages would not be adequate • Will not be granted for a number of reasons: – If constant supervision of the court is required, Ryan v Mutual Tontine – In contracts of personal service – Page One Records Ltd v Britton – To enforce an unfair contract, Walters v Morgan – If it will cause the defendant hardship, Patel v Ali – In the absence of mutuality, Price v Strange Injunction: • Court order instructing somebody to: – Refrain from doing something - prohibitory injunction – Do something - mandatory injunction • An injunction will not be awarded for a party to complete a personal service, Page One Records Ltd v Britton • An injunction can be: – permanent/perpetual – temporary/interim Credit any other relevant content AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: • Specific performance guarantees justice is served when the subject matter of the contract is unique. Damages cannot and do not act as a substitute in such situations, Falcke v Gray • Specific performance does not guarantee justice is served as it is not generally available in employment contracts however it would be very difficult for the court to oversee an order in such circumstances • Specific performance does not guarantee justice is served if the claimant delays too long in seeking the remedy. An additional issue is how long is ‘too long’? However, the maxim delay defeats equity does protect the defendant and provide some justice • Specific performance guarantees justice to the defendant as the court will not award the remedy if it would cause undue hardship i.e. harm the defendant • Specific performance ensures justice as it will not be granted unless mutuality between the parties can be achieved. It can only be granted if it is available against both parties ● Specific performance guarantees justice to the defendant in situations where the claimant’s actions are inequitable. If the claimant’s actions are unconscionable, the remedy will be unavailable ● The fact that mandatory injunctions are rarely awarded when overseeing and enforcing them is difficult and restrictive on the defendant ensures justice is served ● An interim injunction may be said to ensure justice is served as it is only granted where the claimant might suffer irreparable harm if forced to wait for the main action. Justice is served as this prevents the breach continuing until the wider issue is resolved ● Justice is not achieved as the burden is on the claimant to demonstrate why damages would be an insufficient remedy. This is a heavy burden. ●  Justice may not be guaranteed in terms of both as the burden is on the claimant to demonstrate why damages would be an insufficient remedy. This is a heavy burden. Credit any other relevant analysis and application and evaluation AO1 AO2 AO3 Answer

text: The restrictions on minors entering contracts are justified. Assess the validity of this statement.
title: The restrictions on minors entering contracts are justified. Assess the validity of this statement.
msText: The restrictions on minors entering contracts are justified. Assess the validity of this statement. Use Table B to mark candidate responses to this question. AO1 out of 12 marks. AO2 out of 5 marks. AO3 out of 8 marks. Indicative content: Responses may include: AO1 Knowledge and understanding Contracts valid and enforceable against the minor: • Contracts for necessaries; s3 Sale of Goods Act 1979, Nash v Inman, Chapple v Cooper, Fawcett v Smethurst • Beneficial contracts of service, Clements v London and NWRC, De Francesco v Barnum, Doyle v White City Stadium, Clements v London and North Western Railway Co, Proform Sports Management Ltd v Proactive Sports Management Contracts voidable by minors: • Voidable contracts include contracts to lease property, purchase shares, enter a partnership, marriage settlement • Minor can avoid a voidable contract at any time before reaching the age of 18 years, and for a reasonable time afterwards, Edwards v Carter, Steinberg v Scala (Leeds) Ltd, Corpe v Overton Void and unenforceable contracts: • All other contracts are considered void and unenforceable against the minor.  The other party will be bound. • Minors’ Contract Act 1987: s2(1) a guarantee can be enforced, s3 restitution. Credit any other relevant content AO2 Analysis and application and AO3 Evaluation: • The rules regarding contracts for necessaries adequately protect minors. A minor is able to enter contracts for items such as food and clothing but they will only be bound if the goods and services are necessaries to their station in life and suit their actual requirements. • An unscrupulous adult/business will not take advantage of a minor by overcharging. If a good or service is considered necessaries the minor is only obliged to pay a reasonable price • The restrictions also ensure that a minor is only obliged to pay for goods actually supplied. • The law is protective rather than restrictive as contracts for necessaries will not be enforceable if the terms of the contract are prejudicial to the minor’s best interests. • The rules on beneficial contracts of service allow minors to enter contracts to support themselves financially in terms of education and employment but they are protected as if any of the terms act to the minor’s detriment they will automatically invalidate the contract of service • The restrictions in place regarding voidable contracts protect a minor due to their onerous nature. • The ability to repudiate all obligations under a voidable contract stops a minor committing themselves to a long-term recurring obligation and being taken advantage of • The MCA allows a minor to enter a contract with the backing of a guarantor (s2) and protects the minor as the obligations will be enforceable against the guarantor. Credit any other relevant analysis and application and evaluation AO1 AO2 AO3

text: Rick is a chemistry teacher at Barchester Academy. He requests more protective eye goggles for the chemistry laboratories as there are not enough for all the students. The academy tells him that they have been ordered. Until they arrive, he is told to conduct experiments in the laboratory with small groups so that all students can be protected. Rick is concerned that he will not be able to complete teaching his course by the end of the school year, so he conducts some experiments with the entire class. During one of the experiments Rick drops a container of chemicals. One student, Elaine, is seriously injured when the chemical goes into her eye. She is not wearing any goggles as there are not enough for the whole class. She is taken to hospital and doctors say that she will need significant treatment to make a full recovery. Instead of storing containers of chemicals in a locked cupboard, Rick keeps them in his office. A student enters the office without permission when Rick is not there and knocks over the containers. The chemicals leak into an adjoining property used by Marketing Company X (MCX). The chemicals damage the property and as a result, MCX is forced to close its business for several days. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Naomi’s neighbour John is building a new house on his land. In order to install water pipes, he is digging under Naomi’s garden without her permission. text: Police Constable (PC) Conor is driving his police car in pursuit of a gang of armed robbers. He switches on the car’s siren and drives at speed through a junction where the traffic lights are red. Helen approaches the junction from a different direction. The traffic lights are green and as Helen drives forward, her car is hit by the police car. Helen does not hear the police siren because she is listening to loud music. Helen is injured and trapped in her car. The emergency services are called. Helen is taken to Barchester hospital by ambulance where she is initially treated by Dr Frank, a newly qualified junior doctor. He does not identify the symptoms of internal bleeding. The next day Helen is examined by a senior doctor who finds that she has sustained severe damage to her kidney. It is too late to treat the injury and her kidney must be removed. Helen is unable to return to work for six months. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Tony inherits a collection of paintings and antique vases. He does not know how much the collection is worth, so he contacts XYZ gallery to request a valuation. XYZ asks a member of staff, Jane, to examine the collection. Jane is a very experienced dealer in paintings, but her knowledge of antique vases is limited. Therefore, XYZ instructs her not to offer any advice in relation to the value of Tony’s antique vases. Jane visits Tony and values the collection of paintings. As she is leaving, Tony asks her about an antique vase. Jane examines it briefly and informs him that it is a modern copy and of no value. Tony donates the vase to a charity. The charity sells the vase at a fundraising auction. The vase is in fact a very rare original. Several people at the auction recognise its value and the price increases as they bid against each other to buy it. A week later, Tony receives a letter from the charity thanking him for donating the vase, which sold for £50 000. Tony is shocked as he would not have donated the vase if he had known its true value. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Franco is cycling home from work when he is pushed off his bicycle by Maria. As he lies on the ground, Maria takes a bottle of clear liquid from her bag and, telling him it contains acid, demands money. Franco hands over all his money and Maria throws the bottle at him as she runs away. It hits him on the shoulder but causes no injury. Franco shouts at her that he will ‘make her pay’ next time he sees her. The police later tell Franco that the bottle actually contained water. The next day, Maria goes to a local supermarket. She fills a shopping basket with goods and walks towards the exit. Terry, a security guard, sees that she has not paid for the goods and stops her from leaving. He takes Maria to the office and leaves her there while he calls the police. Maria sits in the office for an hour, unaware that Terry is standing outside. The police arrive and take Maria into custody. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: John lives in an apartment building. He works from home for a technology company. Olivia lives in the apartment above. Every morning, Olivia takes part in an online exercise class. When John starts work at 08:00, he can hear Olivia exercising and the voice of the instructor. He tells Olivia that the noise is very annoying, but she says that she has no intention of giving up her exercise class. Olivia is an opera singer. She practises her singing every evening. The sound of her singing makes it impossible for John to relax after work. One evening, Olivia is still practising at 23:00. John knocks on her door and shouts that if the singing continues, he will break down the door and make her stop. Olivia ignores John, and she continues to sing. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Steve applies for a job with AB Ltd (ABL). He asks his employer, XY Ltd (XYL), to send a reference to ABL. Ann, a manager in XYL, is responsible for providing references. She supplies a reference which indicates that Steve had a poor employment performance record. Steve is informed by ABL that his application has not been successful. When he requests further information, he is informed that the reason was the negative reference provided by XYL. Steve contacts XYL and points out that his work record was excellent. Ann checks the reference she provided and realises that she had looked at the employment record of a different employee with a very similar name to Steve. Ann admits that she should have provided a positive reference to ABL. Steve left his job at XYL as he expected to secure employment with ABL. He is unable to pay his rent and is in severe financial difficulty. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

Kate tells Liz that she has heard stories of treasure buried in the grounds of the castle. Kate takes some tools from her bag and starts to dig. As she is digging, Sean arrives and tells them both to leave immediately. Liz leaves, but Kate refuses. Sean grabs Kate and pushes her off his land. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Anne has recently inherited a large amount of money. She asks her friend Dan, an architect, if a plot of land near her house would be suitable for building. Anne would like to purchase the land and build some houses, which she hopes to sell for a substantial profit. Dan advises her, free of charge, that the land is suitable for building. Anne purchases the land for £1 million. She then discovers that the land has regularly flooded in recent years and is therefore unsuitable for building. Anne cannot build on the land and is unable to sell it. While driving to a meeting at the bank, Anne replies to a text on her smartphone. She loses control of the car and crashes into a wall. Anne is not injured but the wall collapses and traps Jim, who is working in his garden. Jim’s wife, Mia, hears the noise of the crash and runs out of the house to find Jim lying on the ground covered in blood. Mia comforts Jim while they wait for the ambulance. Jim makes a full recovery but Mia is traumatised and is unable to return to work as a self-employed accountant for six months. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Rio owns a large house with extensive grounds. He is converting the house into a small hotel. The house and grounds are not yet open to the public. Rio erects a fence around the construction site and displays a ‘No Entry’ sign on the locked gate. Rio is aware that a number of local teenagers have found a gap in the fence and have been entering the site late at night. Nat, aged 16, and his friends climb through the gap in the fence one night. Nat falls into a deep uncovered hole. He is taken to hospital with a head injury and a broken arm. His new smartphone is broken in the fall and cannot be repaired. The next day, Rio goes to the hospital to enquire about Nat’s condition. He is confronted by Nat’s father, Pete, who tells him that if they were not in the hospital he would ‘give him a good beating’ for what has happened to Nat. Rio tries to leave but Pete stands in his way. Rio pushes Pete aside and runs out of the hospital. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Pavel is driving his truck on a busy motorway in excess of the speed limit. Whilst changing lanes to overtake without using the truck’s indicator, Pavel’s truck hits a car driven by Sean. Both drivers stop their vehicles by the side of the motorway, to inspect the damage and exchange insurance details. Sean’s car is badly damaged. In his rush to stop after the collision, Sean does not move his car completely off the motorway. As he and Pavel are about to get back into their vehicles, a car driven by Becky hits Sean’s car. Sean and Pavel are trapped between Sean’s car and Pavel’s truck. They are both bleeding heavily and shouting for help. Becky is uninjured but is traumatised. Cara, a nurse, sees the incident and stops to help. However, she is unable to reach the injured parties trapped between the vehicles. When the emergency services arrive, they take Sean and Pavel to hospital. Cara has been very upset since the incident as she believes that she should have done more to help. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Anna opens a bakery and shop. There is a step at the entrance to the shop, so, to warn customers, Anna makes and displays a small but colourful sign at the door which reads ‘Watch your step!’. Val is going to her mother’s 80th birthday party and has forgotten to buy her a birthday cake. Val rushes into the shop and is relieved to find that Anna has a suitable cake. She pays for it and quickly turns to leave. As she does so, she trips on the step. She falls, crushes the cake and breaks her leg. The good reputation of Anna’s bakery results in a contract to supply several supermarkets. To fulfil these orders, Anna extends the operating hours of the bakery so that production continues throughout the night. Paul has lived in an apartment opposite the bakery for several years. He is now frequently woken at night by the noise of delivery trucks. The air conditioning in the bakery is not working so windows are kept open and Paul can hear the loud music played by the staff. He complains to Anna that the new operating hours are disruptive. Anna says that there is nothing she can do if she is to keep customers happy and her business profitable. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: John is the company accountant for XYZ. He has recently prepared the annual financial statements for the company, which show that it has made a significant profit. John meets his friend Frank for lunch. Frank tells John that he has inherited a large sum of money. John says that XYZ has had an exceptionally good year and that he believes that the company will grow and become more profitable every year. Frank invests all his inheritance in XYZ. The following year XYZ goes out of business. John had not taken into consideration a number of recent loans obtained by the company when he prepared the financial statements. In fact, the company was not making a profit but was trading at a loss. However, this was not reflected in the financial statements prepared by John. Frank has lost his entire investment. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Barchester Council decides to install a charging point for electric vehicles in its main car park. The council hires Andy, who quotes the lowest price for the work. The council is satisfied that Andy is knowledgeable and experienced enough as an electrician to do the work, even though he has had no previous experience of installing vehicle charging points. Andy completes the installation work, but customers soon start to complain that their vehicles are not charging properly. Colm, the chairman of the council, uses the charging point to charge his own car and receives an electric shock, resulting in minor burns. The council contacts a specialist company to inspect Andy’s work and is advised to close the charging point until it has been inspected. Liam, aged 13, goes to the car park. There is a sign on the charging point which says, ‘out of use’. Nevertheless, Liam uses it to charge his electric scooter, which overheats and catches fire. As he runs from the car park, he falls and breaks his arm. His electric scooter is destroyed in the fire. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Amy is shopping in Barchester superstore. As she is leaving, she is stopped by Will, a security guard. He asks her if she has paid for the items in her bag. Amy refuses to answer him. She becomes angry and shouts at Will that if he asks her again, she will hit him. Will calls the store manager, Daniel, for assistance. While he is waiting, Will asks Amy again if she has paid for the items. She pushes past Will, causing him to fall to the ground and break his wrist. Daniel arrives and stands in front of Amy to stop her leaving. He says he has called the police and they will arrive soon. Daniel takes Amy to the staff room and tells her to wait for the police. After an hour of waiting, Amy checks the door. She realises that it is not locked, so she leaves the staff room and exits the superstore. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.

text: Matt travels abroad frequently for work meetings. When he is away, he rents out his house to guests on a short-term basis. Matt has built a large balcony that overlooks the garden of the adjoining property which is owned by Sally. Matt has installed outdoor cooking facilities on the balcony and a heater so that his guests can use it at all times. After a few months, Sally complains to Matt that she is not comfortable using her garden anymore as the balcony is in constant use and the guests can see into her garden. She is also concerned by the noise they make and the strong smells of the outdoor cooking. Matt tells her that they are paying guests and they can do what they want in his house. The next time the house is rented out, Matt is contacted by Tony, a guest. Tony complains that he was unable to sleep throughout the weekend as there was constant hammering on the walls at night. When Matt returns and speaks to Sally, she tells him that she can do what she wants in her house. Advise the parties of their rights, responsibilities and potential remedies.
